opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to the difference between bits and atoms.

On the computational side, the whole loop lives in software. If you're training a model to predict protein structures, or screening millions of candidate molecules, or simulating materials properties, you can iterate in hours. You change a hyperparameter, rerun, see the result. And critically, you're riding on infrastructure that someone else already built and keeps improving: GPUs get faster, frameworks get better, open datasets like the Protein Data Bank were accumulated over decades. AlphaFold didn't have to wait for anyone to build new hardware. It had fifty years of curated crystallography data sitting there.

Physical automated labs don't get that free ride. Every experiment is constrained by real chemistry and real physics. A reaction takes the time it takes. A cell culture grows at the speed biology allows. And the automation itself is genuinely hard. Liquid handling, sample transfer, dealing with a powder that clumps or a solution that crystallizes in a tube: these are messy, long-tail problems. A human chemist adapts without thinking. A robot needs that case anticipated, engineered, and tested.

There's also a standardization problem. In software, a Python environment is basically the same everywhere. In wet labs, every instrument vendor has its own protocols and data formats, and lots of equipment was never designed to be driven by a machine. So a big part of building a self-driving lab is just plumbing: getting the instruments to talk to each other and produce clean, structured data.

And then there's cost and scale. If a computational idea fails, you've lost some compute time. If a physical platform fails, you may have spent millions on hardware and years on integration. That naturally makes the field more cautious and slower to iterate.

But I'd frame it as a temporary imbalance, not a permanent one. Computational models are increasingly bottlenecked by data, especially high-quality, consistent experimental data, including negative results, which almost never get published. The models can propose far more hypotheses than we can validate. So the real value comes from closing the loop: AI proposes, automated labs test, the results feed back into the model. Whoever makes the physical side reliable and scalable is going to unlock much more of what the computational side promises. Right now the brain is ahead of the hands, and the next phase is about catching the hands up.

r001.rationale: The response says software experiments can iterate quickly and show results, but it does not attribute faster development to progress being easier to measure.

r002.rationale: It discusses lab automation generally, but does not identify robots specialized for particular experimental steps as a form of AutoLab.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest answer is that bits are cheap and atoms are expensive, and that gap compounds at every step.

On the computational side, a model like AlphaFold or a materials-discovery model can be trained once and then run millions of times, essentially for free. The data already exists in databases, the iteration loop is minutes, and the whole ML community's tooling, from GPUs to open-source frameworks, transfers directly. So when someone has a good idea, the time from idea to result is days.

A physical lab is the opposite. Every experiment costs real reagents, real instrument time, and real failures. The hardware is bespoke: a robot arm that handles liquid samples doesn't help you grow a crystal or anneal a thin film. Each new chemistry or material class needs new fixtures, new safety protocols, new calibration. There's no equivalent of "just scale up the cluster." And the data these labs generate is messy, small, and hard to standardize, so it feeds back into the models much more slowly than people hoped.

There's also a talent and incentive issue. The people who are good at automation engineering, at building reliable robotic systems, are mostly in industry working on cars and warehouses, not in chemistry departments. And academic incentives reward the paper, not the robust platform that would let the next person reuse your setup.

So I don't think the gap is surprising. The computation side has been riding the same exponential as the rest of AI, while the physical side is fundamentally limited by how fast you can move matter around and how many distinct things you need to engineer. The interesting question is whether the computational progress eventually pulls the physical side along, by telling labs exactly which few experiments are worth running instead of brute-forcing thousands.

r001.rationale: The response points to existing data and fast computational iteration, and says physical-lab data is messy and slow to feed back. It does not clearly attribute the faster progress to computational progress being easier to measure.

r002.rationale: The response describes lab robots as bespoke and specialized for particular tasks, but does not identify these robots as a form of AutoLab.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is the cost and speed of getting feedback. In a computational workflow, once you have the data and a way to evaluate results, you can run many experiments in parallel. If something fails, you change the code and try again. The whole cycle can be relatively fast.

In a physical laboratory, every iteration has to happen in the real world. You need to prepare samples, operate instruments, wait for reactions, and measure results. Some processes simply take time. Automation can reduce the manual work, but it can’t make a reaction that takes several hours finish instantly.

There’s also an integration problem. A laboratory isn’t one machine—it’s a collection of instruments and procedures, often with different interfaces. A scientist handles many small exceptions almost without thinking: a sample looks unusual, something needs cleaning, an instrument needs recalibration. Making an automated system handle those situations reliably is difficult.

So computational AI can often advance by improving one part of a workflow, while an automated laboratory needs the entire chain to work. And the two are connected: when a computational prediction needs experimental validation, it encounters those same physical bottlenecks.

r001.rationale: The response links computational AI’s faster progress to having data and a way to evaluate results, enabling rapid feedback and iteration.

r002.rationale: The response discusses laboratory instruments and automation generally, but does not identify robots specialized for particular experimental steps as a form of AutoLab.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is the speed and cost of the feedback loop. In computational research, once you have the data and a way to evaluate results, you can run many experiments in parallel. If something fails, you change the code and try again. You can also build on existing software and computing infrastructure.

In a physical laboratory, every experiment has to deal with the real world. You have to prepare samples, calibrate instruments, handle materials, and wait for reactions or measurements. A robot can execute a procedure, but making that procedure reliable across different conditions is much harder. Even a small variation in a sample can affect the result.

There’s also a difference in standardization. Software systems have relatively mature interfaces. Laboratory equipment often comes from different manufacturers, with different interfaces, and many procedures still depend on a researcher’s hands-on judgment. Connecting all of that into a system that can operate independently takes substantial engineering.

So the bottleneck isn’t just whether the AI is smart enough to propose an experiment. It’s whether the laboratory can execute that experiment reliably and return useful feedback. Computational AI can improve on a much shorter cycle, while physical automation has to advance at the pace of both engineering and the experiment itself.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts computational experiments’ faster feedback loops with the time and cost of physical experiments, but does not clearly attribute computational AI’s faster development to the relative ease of measuring its progress.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots executing procedures generally, but does not identify robots specialized for particular experimental steps as a form of AutoLab.
